findings.summary: THE FIX CLOSED ONE DISJUNCT OF EACH GUARD, NOT THE GUARD. Four decode bounds are written `X < 0 || X > <limit>`, and every test added this round feeds only a POSITIVE-wide value (`WIDE_ONE` = 0x1_0000_0001), which the `> <limit>` half alone refuses. The `< 0` half of all four is unconstrained, and for two of them dropping it flips REFUSE into ACCEPT-WITH-WRONG-DATA. SURVIVING MUTATION 1, Checkpoint.java:189 `partitionId < 0 || partitionId > Integer.MAX_VALUE` -> `partitionId > Integer.MAX_VALUE`: whole :format:test suite green (19 result XMLs, 0 failures, --rerun-tasks). Measured directly: a stream entry whose partitionId is the full-width uvarint 81 80 80 80 f0 ff ff ff ff 01 (= 0xFFFFFFFF00000001, negative as a long, 1 as an int) decodes to `Checkpoint[sequence=1, streams={RunKey[...0001, partitionId=1]=StreamOffsets[90,10]}, pods={poda=1}]` -- ACCEPTED, one stream's offsets attributed to another, no exception. That is tr-8 verbatim, one bit over. SURVIVING MUTATION 2, Checkpoint.java:206 `podCount < 0 || podCount > c.remaining()` -> `podCount > c.remaining()`: suite green; an object ending in a full-width negative pod count decodes to `pods={}` -- every lastAppliedFlushSeq silently dropped rather than the object refused. The decode() javadoc at Checkpoint.java:159-160 names 'a partitionId that reads negative' as one of the five measured routes, so this is again a claim stated in a comment with no test behind it. ALSO SURVIVING, but message-only (still IOException, so lower harm): `streamCount < 0` dropped (Checkpoint.java:174) and `podLen < 0` dropped (Checkpoint.java:217). One test feeding a full-width negative varint into each of the four fields closes the shape rather than a fifth instance of it.
findings.failure_scenario: A later reader simplifies `partitionId < 0 || partitionId > Integer.MAX_VALUE` to `partitionId > Integer.MAX_VALUE` on the entirely reasonable ground that a uvarint cannot be negative -- and the podLen guard one field over has the identical shape, so both get 'simplified' together. `./gradlew :format:test` stays green in every one of the 19 classes. M4.9 then reads a torn checkpoint, gets a valid-looking Checkpoint back with partitionId 1 instead of the real stream and with pods={} instead of the real flush sequences, and resumes one stream from another stream's nextOffset while re-applying flushes it had already applied. Nothing throws, so the `catch (IOException)` M4.9 is being written against never fires.

findings.summary: theMapsAreCOPIEDSoALaterMutationCannotReachTheRecord names 'the maps' and pins the unmodifiability of only ONE of them. SURVIVING MUTATION, Checkpoint.java:75: `pods = Collections.unmodifiableMap(new LinkedHashMap<>(pods))` -> `pods = new LinkedHashMap<>(pods)`. Whole :format:test suite green (19 XMLs, 0 failures, --rerun-tasks). Measured: `new Checkpoint(1, Map.of(), Map.of("poda", 1L)).pods().put("podz", 9L)` then returns `{poda=1, podz=9}` instead of throwing UnsupportedOperationException. The test asserts `c.pods()).hasSize(1)` (which pins the COPY) but the UnsupportedOperationException assertion on the next line is made against `c.streams()` only. Same 'the name claims both, the body exercises one' shape as tr-7, which this round fixed for the duplicate guard.
findings.failure_scenario: A refactor drops the unmodifiable wrapper on `pods` -- plausibly while adding a builder or while making the copy lazy -- and the suite stays green. A caller holding a decoded Checkpoint then mutates `checkpoint.pods()` in place; because the record is a value type shared by whatever M4.8b and M4.9 hand it to, one component's edit is visible to every other holder of the same instance, and the record's own javadoc promise that the copy is defensive is false for half the record.

findings.summary: The header-length guard's BOUNDARY is unconstrained, and it is the last thing standing between a truncated object and an unchecked exception. SURVIVING MUTATION, Checkpoint.java:136: `if (bytes.length < 8)` -> `if (bytes.length < 7)`. Whole :format:test suite green (19 XMLs, 0 failures, --rerun-tasks). Measured: a 7-byte array starting 42 43 4b 50 then makes `b.getInt(4)` throw `IndexOutOfBoundsException` out of a method declared `throws IOException`. bytesThatAreNotACheckpointAreRefusedRatherThanMisread only ever passes `new byte[]{1,2,3}` (length 3) and a full-length object with a broken magic, so no test sits anywhere near the 8-byte edge. This is the same checked-vs-unchecked contract that aTORNObjectIsAnIOExceptionRatherThanAnUncheckedOne and the `catch (IllegalArgumentException)` wrap at Checkpoint.java:150 exist to guarantee, and the guard predates this round rather than being added by it.
findings.failure_scenario: An off-by-one in the header-length guard (or a later header that grows to 12 bytes without the constant following it) lets a 4-to-7-byte truncated PUT reach `b.getInt(4)`. M4.9's `catch (IOException)` does not catch IndexOutOfBoundsException, so recovery dies with an unchecked exception on a partially-written object instead of treating it as corrupt -- the exact failure mode this commit spends a paragraph of Checkpoint.java:151-161 closing for the IllegalArgumentException route.

findings.summary: MUTATION SCORE, measured this round over format/src/main/java/binjava/format/Checkpoint.java with the whole :format:test suite, `--rerun-tasks`, and pass/fail read from build/test-results/test/*.xml per mutant: 38 mutants applied, 28 killed, 10 survived = 73.7% killed, below testing.md rule 9's 80% floor. Round 2 measured 63.6% (7 of 11), so it improved. Six of the ten survivors are bound-WEAKENINGS that leave the object still refused with an IOException and change only the operator message -- streamCount `/18` -> no divisor, `/18` -> `/9`, podCount `c.remaining()` -> `2*c.remaining()`, podLen `c.remaining()` -> `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, and the streamCount/podLen `< 0` halves. Treating those six as equivalent mutants gives 28/32 = 87.5%, which clears the floor -- but testing.md rule 9 requires a surviving mutant to be killed OR argued in baselines/mutants.txt, and no such entry is staged, so 73.7% is the number of record. The four non-equivalent survivors are tr-10 (x2), tr-11 and tr-12. Notably, the pod-count message assertion added this round pins the message but not the bound: `podCount > c.remaining()` -> `podCount > 2 * c.remaining()` survives.
findings.failure_scenario: check-mutants.sh does not exist, so nothing in the tree records that this file sits at 73.7%. The next change to Checkpoint.java is measured against no baseline, a survivor introduced then looks identical to one inherited from here, and the 80% floor stays an aspiration that no commit is ever held to -- which is precisely the 'green gate reported by someone who did not run it' failure non-negotiable 4 names.
